title: Victoria's landmark work-from-home laws delayed
text:
By NICHOLAS COMINO, POLITICAL REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  11:20 AEST, 10 September 2026   |  Updated:  11:20 AEST, 10 September 2026

6

View  comments

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll will water down and delay Labor's controversial work-from-home laws, giving employers greater power to reject or revoke remote-working arrangements after backlash from businesses.

The government will move amendments on Thursday, pushing back the proposed employee right to work from home for at least two days a week until July 1 next year.

Small businesses will be granted an extra six-month exemption, with the scheme not applying to them until January 1, 2028.

Under the revised laws, employers will be allowed to consider their operational requirements when ruling on work-from-home requests, including whether remote work could have a 'material adverse impact' on productivity or efficiency.

Previously, the government had used the threshold of 'significant adverse impact', but the new wording gives businesses broader leeway to reject requests.

The move represents a major concession by Carroll, who has sought to position Labor as more business-friendly since taking over from Jacinta Allan.

Weeks after becoming premier, Carroll withdrew the bill from debate and reopened talks with employers after industry concerns.

The changes will also give bosses the right to revoke existing work-from-home arrangements if circumstances change and a worker is no longer eligible, or if the arrangement is no longer deemed reasonable.

Ben Carroll (pictured) has unveiled a watered down version of his work from home laws

Businesses will have 28 days to reply to work-from-home requests, up from the previously proposed 21-day deadline.

The new version of the bill also pares back the costs for businesses. Employers will only need to provide essential hardware, software and secure access to workplace IT systems, while internet costs will remain the responsibility of employees.

The bill will prohibit workers from stacking the new entitlement with any existing work-from-home rights unless their employer agrees.

Eligibility for the scheme will be limited to those whose main home is in Victoria. The amendments also spell out how the 40 per cent work-from-home entitlement will work for part-time staff, applied on a pro-rata basis.

A review of the legislation will now be launched within 18 months of its start, rather than after three years as previously planned.

In a joint statement, major industry groups recognised Carroll's willingness to engage but said the amendments did not address what they saw as fundamental problems with the bill.

'We acknowledge the Premier's willingness to consult with business groups. However, despite Premier Ben Carroll offering a significant range of amendments, those amendments do not fix a fundamentally flawed law that will risk Victoria's economy and send jobs interstate,' the groups said.

'The Bill should be abandoned, and no amendment can fix its fundamental problems.

Business groups have called on the government to abandon the work from home legislation

How should Victoria balance workers' rights to flexibility with businesses’ need for control and productivity?

'We consider that the passing of this legislation leaves the Government's commitment to 'grow the economy' in tatters.

'There is no clear plan to turn around Victoria's deteriorating economic performance, which puts it behind every other state in the nation.

'Victoria already has the highest unemployment rate in the nation, and at a time when households and businesses are under pressure, Victoria neither needs nor wants this legislation.'

The groups also cited new legal advice released by the Property Council of Australia, which found the bill was inconsistent with the Fair Work Act and could be rendered invalid under the Constitution.

'Today the Property Council of Australia released independent constitutional law advice finding the bill is inconsistent with the Fair Work Act and would be rendered invalid under the Australian Constitution.

'This raises serious questions about whether the Government is proceeding with legislation that may not withstand legal scrutiny.

'Simply put, the passage of this bill would threaten jobs, discourage investment and add costs Victoria cannot afford.'
